ch01.question: What can we learn by looking at the whole economy?
ch01.introduction: Start with income, jobs, and prices. Discover how economists move from facts to models, then use those models to ask new questions.

ch02.question: How do we measure an entire economy?
ch02.introduction: Follow production, spending, and income through the national accounts. Learn what GDP measures, how prices change, and what the headline numbers leave out.

ch03.question: How did the world become so much richer?
ch03.introduction: Trace living standards across countries and centuries. Explore the power of compounding and the striking differences in when sustained growth began.

ch04.question: Why do some economies produce so much more?
ch04.introduction: Build a production model from capital, labor, and productivity. Compare its predictions with the data to see how much of the income gap it can explain.

ch05.question: Can saving more make a country richer?
ch05.introduction: Operate the Solow model and watch capital accumulate. Explore steady states, transition dynamics, and the limits of growth driven by investment alone.

ch06.question: What keeps economic growth going?
ch06.introduction: Ideas can be used by many people at once. Explore how this changes the economics of production and why research can sustain rising living standards.

ch07.question: Why are some people unemployed even when jobs exist?
ch07.introduction: Connect wages and employment to labor supply and demand. Then follow workers into and out of jobs to understand persistent unemployment.

ch08.question: Why does money lose its purchasing power?
ch08.introduction: Measure inflation in the data and connect prices to money and output. Explore the quantity theory, real interest rates, and the costs of inflation.

ch09.question: Why does the economy move in ups and downs?
ch09.introduction: Separate the long-run path of output from short-run fluctuations. Use data on output, jobs, and inflation to describe what happens in a recession.

ch10.question: What made the financial crisis and pandemic so disruptive?
ch10.introduction: Compare two very different downturns. Trace housing, financial markets, output, and employment to see how each shock spread through the economy.

ch11.question: How do interest rates change spending and output?
ch11.introduction: Build the IS curve from the national income identity. Change demand and borrowing costs to see why short-run output moves.

ch12.question: How can a central bank bring inflation down?
ch12.introduction: Connect monetary policy to the IS and Phillips curves. Follow the path of output and inflation when the central bank changes the interest rate.

ch13.question: Can policy cushion an economic shock?
ch13.introduction: Bring the short-run model together in the AS/AD diagram. Explore how policy rules, expectations, and different shocks shape the adjustment.

ch14.question: What happens when the financial system stops working?
ch14.introduction: Add risk premiums and financial frictions to the short-run model. Examine how a credit crisis, deflation, and policy constraints can deepen a recession.

ch15.question: How do modern models explain business cycles?
ch15.introduction: Meet the agents, shocks, and frictions inside DSGE models. Explore how productivity, labor markets, and sticky prices shape the economy’s response.

ch16.question: How do households decide what to spend today?
ch16.introduction: Spread income and wealth across a lifetime. Use a two-period model to explore consumption smoothing, patience, and the role of interest rates.

ch17.question: What makes a new investment worthwhile?
ch17.introduction: Compare the return on capital with its cost. Connect firms’ investment choices to interest rates, taxes, stock prices, and housing.

ch18.question: How do today’s deficits shape tomorrow’s choices?
ch18.introduction: Follow government spending, taxes, and borrowing through the budget constraint. Explore debt dynamics and the choices involved in financing public spending.

ch19.question: Why do countries trade—and who gains?
ch19.introduction: Work through comparative advantage and the gains from exchange. Connect trade balances to saving, investment, and borrowing from the rest of the world.

ch20.question: What moves a currency’s value?
ch20.introduction: Compare purchasing power across countries and returns across currencies. Explore exchange rates, international finance, and policy in an open economy.

ch21.question: What have we learned—and what remains unresolved?
ch21.introduction: Bring the book’s main lessons together. Revisit living standards, growth, inflation, and stabilization, then consider the questions macroeconomics still needs to answer.

appA.question: How can you run economics with Python and AI?
appA.introduction: Open a notebook in Google Colab, run its code, and make it your own. Learn how to ask an AI assistant for help and check the answers it gives.

appB.question: Where can you find the data behind the questions?
appB.introduction: Download macroeconomic series directly with Python. Learn how to choose sources, compare definitions, and prepare data for analysis.

appC.question: Which mathematical tools make the models clearer?
appC.introduction: Review percentages, logarithms, growth rates, and the algebra behind the book. Connect each tool to the economic questions it helps answer.

appD.question: How much growth comes from inputs—and how much from productivity?
appD.introduction: Use growth and development accounting to separate capital, labor, and productivity. Compare changes over time and differences in living standards across countries.

appE.question: Are poorer countries catching up?
appE.introduction: Derive convergence from the Solow model, then test it across countries. Compare growth regressions with changes in the dispersion of incomes.

appF.question: Does human capital explain the income gap?
appF.introduction: Add schooling to the Solow model. Rebuild the Mankiw–Romer–Weil analysis and compare its findings with more recent international data.

appG.question: Do better institutions cause greater prosperity?
appG.introduction: Revisit the Acemoglu–Johnson–Robinson study. Explore why correlation is not enough and how historical instruments are used to study institutions and income.

appH.question: How can you build and estimate a DSGE model?
appH.introduction: Use Python and Snowdrop to write, solve, simulate, and estimate dynamic models. Let the data help determine parameters and inspect the response to shocks.

appI.question: How does an estimated economy respond to shocks?
appI.introduction: Work with the Smets–Wouters model in Python. Recompute impulse responses and explore the roles of sticky wages, sticky prices, and monetary policy.
